name: Carcassonne meeple scarcity (7 meeples across 70-90 tiles)
one_line: Every player gets exactly 7 meeples for a ~70-90 tile game, so roughly half your turns you must decide whether to place a follower at all
take_what: Hard cap of a small placeable-resource pool (7 meeples) shared across a much larger tile-draw pool, so 'do I commit here' is a real question on most turns, not just 'where do I place'

name: Carcassonne invisible opportunity cost of early meeple spend
one_line: A meeple spent on a 2-point road in turn 4 is the meeple you needed for a 12-point city close in turn 14 - the cost of over-committing early is invisible until mid-game
take_what: Make early low-value placements quietly consume a scarce resource whose true cost (a missed late high-value capture window) only becomes visible turns later - creates retroactive tension without any new UI

name: Carcassonne farmer majority flip via merging fields
one_line: Placing a follower in a separate, unconnected field and later connecting it to an opponent's field via a new tile can flip or share majority and steal all their end-game farmer points
take_what: A placement that looks isolated/wasted on turn N can become a delayed pincer that flips control of a distant zone once a connecting tile lands later - the payoff is deferred and depends on future tile draws, creating a 'sleeper threat' read for the opponent
constraint: Limen's adjacency-based influence math would need a way to represent 'unconnected but merge-able later' zones (e.g. via towers or the rift) - closest existing hook is capturing tiles at ≤0 effective influence from anywhere

name: Carcassonne tempo-blocking (road splitters, city-completion denial)
one_line: Players deliberately place tiles that make an opponent's feature harder to close, forcing them to spend future turns fixing it instead of expanding, or trap an opponent's follower in a feature that will never complete
take_what: A placement whose entire value is denial - it does nothing for your own board state, it only removes a completion path or traps an enemy resource in a dead feature - is a first-class strategic option, not a side effect
constraint: Limen already has some denial via capture-at-zero, but pure tempo-blocking (a placement with zero offensive value, purely to deny an enemy combo) is a distinct design lever worth naming explicitly to solve slow-start problem

name: Kingdomino 'blessing in disguise' draft-order coupling
one_line: Designer Bruno Cathala: picking the best tile this round costs you first pick next round (numbered tiles = pick order), so power and turn priority are always in tension with no external balancing needed
take_what: Couple 'strength of thing you take' directly and mechanically to 'your priority/agency next turn' - a single self-balancing lever (tile value = next pick order) replaces any hand-tuned catch-up mechanic
constraint: Limen has simultaneous-ish turn structure (draw 1, place 1) not a draft, but the coupling principle (best card now = worse position next turn) could map onto card draw order, initiative, or influence decay

name: Kingdomino 5x5 boundary + same-color-adjacency constraint
one_line: Cathala deliberately added a hard 5x5 grid boundary specifically because unconstrained placement 'loses tension' - the designer's own words on why constraints are the point, not an obstacle
take_what: Designer explicitly states: giving players total placement freedom kills tension. A hard spatial boundary that forces discard/waste of good draws is a deliberate feature, not a flaw to smooth away
constraint: none - direct design-philosophy citation, relevant to whether Limen's board size/rift should be tightened rather than loosened

name: Kingdomino hate-drafting via visible next-round pick order
one_line: Because pick order is public and tied to tile value, players can deliberately take a tile they don't need purely to deny it to (or worsen the position of) an opponent
take_what: Public, legible future-turn-order information lets players make a 'spite pick' - take something suboptimal for yourself purely to hurt an opponent's plan - a distinct interaction lever from direct combat
constraint: Limen draws 1 card privately per turn rather than a public draft pool, so this needs a shared/visible resource (e.g. a shared card row) to port - bigger structural change than a tweak

name: Kingdomino Monte Carlo AI paper on placement value analysis
one_line: Academic paper builds Monte Carlo search agents for Kingdomino and analyzes which placement heuristics (crown density, territory connectivity) actually drive win rate
take_what: Quantitative confirmation that crown(multiplier)-adjacent territory connectivity is the dominant win-rate driver in Kingdomino, more than raw square count - suggests Limen's influence-adjacency math should similarly reward multiplicative stacking over raw tile count to make placements feel consequential
constraint: academic paper, no reusable code relevant to Limen's stack

name: Carcassonne field-scoring completed-city-count (not tile-count) mechanic
one_line: Farm scoring counts the number of COMPLETED cities bordering the field (3pts each), not the farm's tile area - so a small farm touching 3 finished cities beats a huge farm touching one
take_what: Score a zone by the count of qualifying adjacent COMPLETED structures rather than by raw tile area - rewards positioning near multiple finished assets over sheer size, and creates a race to finish structures before a farm 'locks in' its score
constraint: would require Limen to define a 'completed structure' concept it currently lacks (towers/tiles are individually scored via influence, not grouped structures)
